report.source_text: External examination showed slight proptosis and upward displacement of the right eye (Fig. 1). There was no palpable mass in periorbital area. Hertel exophthalmometry revealed a 3 mm proptosis on the right side. Globe mobility was complete in the left eye, but infraduction and supraduction was comprimised in the right eye. Slit lamp, fundoscopic, Humphrey visual fields and visual evoked potential examinations of both eyes were unremarkable. The intraocular pressure measured by Goldmann tonometer was 15 mm Hg in both eyes.

report.source_text: Orbital computed tomography (CT) scanning showed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle infiltrated by a muscle-density tumor which was about 11 × 17 × 7 mm3 that displaced the globe upward. An axial magnetic resonance images (MRI) view of the orbit revealed a nodule-like tumor derived from the inferior rectus muscle, which was slightly hypo-intense to the extraocular muscles on T1W with a very low central intensity on T2W and a higher intensity along the periphery. Sagittal MRI images showed that the tumor was very close to the optic nerve with almost no gap in between. Enhanced MRI after intravenous contrast administration showed that the tumor was significantly enhanced in the periphery but only slight enhanced in the center (Fig. 2).

Intraoperatively, the tumor was completely separated from muscle tissue since it was pseudoencapsular. The gross specimen exhibited a firm fibrotic nodule-like and pale-colored mass (Fig. 3). There was no significant improvement in globe mobility after surgery; however, a longer term follow-up is required.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of vertical diplopia and decreased visual acuity on upward gaze, accompanied by right eye proptosis and restricted ocular motility. Initial ophthalmological examination confirmed slight proptosis and compromised infraduction and supraduction of the right eye. Orbital CT and MRI revealed an 11x17x7 mm3 tumor infiltrating the right inferior rectus muscle, displacing the globe upward, with characteristic imaging features (hypo-intense on T1W, very low central intensity on T2W with peripheral enhancement). The tumor was surgically removed via a transconjunctival approach. Histopathological analysis of the pseudoencapsulated tumor showed large nested or cord-like cells with small nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasmic particles. Immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of Granular Cell Tumor, showing strong expression of CD68, S100, and vimentin, weak positivity for Ki67, and negativity for CK. Immediate post-operative globe mobility did not significantly improve, and long-term follow-up was noted as required.

Orbital CT showed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle infiltrated by a 11x17x7 mm3 tumor displacing the globe upward.

Orbital MRI revealed a nodule-like tumor derived from the inferior rectus muscle, hypo-intense on T1W, very low central intensity on T2W with higher intensity along the periphery, close to the optic nerve, with significant peripheral enhancement.
The tumor was surgically removed via a transconjunctival approach and was found to be pseudoencapsulated and completely separated from muscle tissue.
Histopathological analysis showed an encapsulated tumor with large nested or cord-like cells, small nuclei, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasmic particles.
Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells strongly expressed CD68, S100, and vimentin, were weakly positive for Ki67, and negative for CK, confirming Granular Cell Tumor.
There was no significant improvement in globe mobility immediately after surgery.

remaining_uncertainties: Long-term follow-up and clinical outcome after surgery.
